title: Occurrence, Preparation, and Properties of Sulfur
lead: Sulfur is found in elemental deposits, in sulfide and sulfate minerals and in natural and volcanic gases. The Frasch process brings it up from underground deposits, and as a nonmetal of group 16 it oxidizes metals and is itself oxidized by more electronegative nonmetals.
objectives: Describe the properties, preparation, and uses of sulfur
summary_html: Sulfur (group 16) reacts with almost all metals and readily forms the sulfide ion, S2−, in which it has as oxidation state of 2−. Sulfur reacts with most nonmetals.
notes: The section keeps as printed the summary’s “has as oxidation state of 2−”, and the key to fs-idm213191488 writes “SO₂, sp² 4+” without its comma.

exercises.prompt: Explain why hydrogen sulfide is a gas at room temperature, whereas water, which has a lower molecular mass, is a liquid.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: compare the intermolecular forces between H<sub>2</sub>S molecules with those between H<sub>2</sub>O molecules, recalling which atoms must carry the hydrogen for hydrogen bonding and how the electronegativity of sulfur compares with that of oxygen; then ask which liquid needs more energy to separate its molecules.

exercises.prompt: Give the hybridization and oxidation state for sulfur in SO<sub>2</sub>, in SO<sub>3</sub>, and in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
Which is the stronger acid, NaHSO<sub>3</sub> or NaHSO<sub>4</sub>?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write the anion that each salt supplies, HSO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> and HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, and count the oxygen atoms bonded to sulfur in each, together with sulfur’s oxidation state; then use the trend in oxyacid strength with the number of oxygen atoms on the central atom.

exercises.prompt: Determine the oxidation state of sulfur in SF<sub>6</sub>, SO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>, and KHS.

answer.solution: SF<sub>6</sub>: S = 6+; SO<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub>: S = 6+; KHS: S = 2−

exercises.prompt: Which is a stronger acid, sulfurous acid or sulfuric acid? Why?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write the formulas H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and the oxidation state of sulfur in each; then use the trend in oxyacid strength: the more oxygen atoms bonded to the central atom, the more electron density is drawn from the O–H bonds.

exercises.prompt: Oxygen forms double bonds in O<sub>2</sub>, but sulfur forms single bonds in S<sub>8</sub>. Why?

answer.solution: Sulfur is able to form double bonds only at high temperatures (substantially endothermic conditions), which is not the case for oxygen.

exercises.prompt: Write two balanced chemical equations in which sulfuric acid acts as an oxidizing agent.

answer.solution: There are many possible answers including: $\text{Cu}(s)+2{\text{H}}_{2}{\text{SO}}_{4}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{CuSO}}_{4}(aq)+{\text{SO}}_{2}(g)+2{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)$ and $\text{C}(s)+2{\text{H}}_{2}{\text{SO}}_{4}(l)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{CO}}_{2}(g)+2{\text{SO}}_{2}(g)+2{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)$

exercises.prompt: Explain why sulfuric acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, which is a covalent molecule, dissolves in water and produces a solution that contains ions.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: recall that sulfuric acid is a strong acid, and write the reaction of an H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> molecule with a water molecule in which a proton moves from the acid to the water; name the ions that form and say why the polar O–H bonds of the acid let this happen.

exercises.prompt: How many grams of Epsom salts (MgSO<sub>4</sub>⋅7H<sub>2</sub>O) will form from 5.0 kg of magnesium?

answer.hint: Convert the mass of magnesium to moles with its molar mass, use the one-to-one ratio of Mg to MgSO<sub>4</sub>⋅7H<sub>2</sub>O, and convert moles of the hydrate to grams with its molar mass.
